c.tx: CASE STUDY 01 / PUBLIC SECTOR RESEARCH + DESIGN
Helping Hungary’s program in shaping a clearer unemployment service
How could the service help a digital citizen understand the whole process while still in it?

For six months, I worked on one of the ‘life event’ projects in Hungary’s Digital Citizenship Program (DÁP): the ‘becoming unemployed’ life event. Me and my team explored how digital services could make the process easier to understand and complete for citizens, while supporting the employment-office staff handling their cases. Research showed that people often struggled to understand the process as a whole. Our response combined visible progress, questions relevant to the person’s circumstances, prefilled information and ways to seek help or interrupt the journey. The work reached a detailed prototype tested with users.

c.tx: A research-informed, iterated prototype used in usability testing. The service’s subsequent rollout and scope is still ongoing.

The team included two product designers, a design lead, a product owner, a senior service designer, researchers, a legal specialist and a copywriter. We worked collaboratively across desk research, social listening, field interviews, in-depth interviews, synthesis, early concepts, ministry discussions, service blueprinting and prototype iteration.

My design responsibility was most concrete in the navigation, the organisation of questions and the detailed experience of moving through the service. I also conducted approximately half of the in-depth interviews. Final approval sat with design leadership and higher-level programme decision-makers.

c.n: sub / The experience we were designing

c.tx: The project concerned the journey of becoming unemployed, including jobseeker registration and the application for unemployment benefits. It connected an individual’s circumstances with an administrative process that involved information gathering, declarations and contact with the employment office.

The aim was to make that journey more manageable for both sides. For citizens, this meant understanding what was relevant to them and what they needed to do next. For staff, the design explored how information prepared digitally could support later handling of the case. The outcome of my involvement was a research-informed prototype; the service’s subsequent rollout and scope remained uncertain.

c.n: sub / Desk research and social listening

c.tx: We began by examining the existing context through desk research and social listening. Early patterns suggested that citizens often had difficulty understanding the process as a whole. A person could know that they needed support without knowing how registration, information requirements and the next administrative step fitted together.

That finding gave us a practical design question: how could the service help a digital citizen understand the whole process while they were still in it? It also gave us something to investigate in interviews. We needed to understand how this uncertainty appeared in different circumstances and how it related to the experience of the people administering the service.

Social listening added accounts expressed outside a formal research interview. We considered those alongside the other research sources as qualitative signals. The purpose was to identify concerns and questions for further investigation; these accounts did not establish how frequently a problem occurred across the entire population.

c.n: sub / A concept before the interviews

c.tx: We developed an early concept before the interviews. It established an initial interaction direction that could subsequently be examined and refined as our understanding of citizens and the service grew.

c.n: The user needed to be able to identify where they were in the process. Navigation and progress information therefore belonged to the core experience. They would help someone understand the relationship between the part they were completing and the wider journey.
c.tx: The user needed to be able to identify where they were in the process. Navigation and progress information therefore belonged to the core experience. They would help someone understand the relationship between the part they were completing and the wider journey.

c.n: Early screening questions would determine which later questions applied to the person’s situation. This would avoid asking people to work through information that was unnecessary in their circumstances. The design depended on understanding the conditions behind each branch, as well as presenting the questions clearly.

c.n: The concept included data prefilled from DÁP for the user to check. This changed the task from entering every detail to reviewing available information and supplying what was still needed. Prefilling did not remove the user’s role in checking the information.

These principles were already present before the in-depth research. The interviews largely reinforced the need for the direction and gave it a richer understanding of the people and working conditions it needed to serve. That continuity matters: the value of the research was in testing the relevance of the initial thinking and informing its detailed development.
Understanding both sides of the service

We conducted short, in-person interviews at employment offices to understand who was arriving and how they experienced the situation. The range of people was broad. Unemployment brought together people with different backgrounds and life circumstances, and the visits made the stress surrounding the process particularly visible.

For the design, this meant that a single assumed user profile would be too narrow. Someone’s ability to use digital products did not necessarily mean they understood the administrative journey. The interface needed to provide orientation and support without assuming prior knowledge of the service.

c.n: sub / In-depth interviews across three perspectives

c.tx: The deeper research included citizens, caseworkers and heads of employment offices. We aimed to cover a wide range of circumstances, and I conducted approximately half of these interviews as part of the shared research work.

Speaking with citizens helped us understand how the process felt from the outside. Interviews with caseworkers and office heads added the perspective of people responsible for delivering the service. Looking across those accounts was essential to a project intended to improve the experience for both groups.

A particularly important difference emerged in how the service was judged. Citizens could describe a poor experience, while staff regarded the service more positively and pointed to the effort they invested in helping people. Both perspectives mattered. The effort involved in providing a service and the experience of receiving it were not being perceived in the same way.

c.n: sub / Turning interview material into design understanding

c.tx: Turning interview material into design understanding

We synthesised the material collaboratively, grouping recurring patterns with the quotations that supported them. Some findings aligned with the earlier research; others added unexpected perspectives. My participation connected first-hand interviewing with the team’s interpretation of the material and the subsequent product work.

The contrast between citizens and staff reinforced the need to make the process easier to understand. Digitalisation offered an opportunity to explain the journey and prepare information more clearly, while taking account of the work performed at the employment office. Whether it would close the perception gap would need evaluation after implementation.

The research also strengthened my understanding of the variety of situations behind the life event. For the product work, I focused on making relevant paths understandable, organising questions coherently and giving people ways to get help. These were concrete ways to respond to the uncertainty and stress that had appeared in the research.

c.n: sub / Taking responsibility for the navigation

c.tx: Taking responsibility for the navigation systems

I developed the navigation across the prototype journey. The early principle that people should understand their position in the process became a detailed design responsibility: the experience needed a coherent structure as the user moved through different groups of questions.

I worked on the grouping of those questions alongside the navigation. Grouping determines how a person understands the task in front of them. In this service, the user also needed to understand how that task related to the rest of the administrative journey. The organisation of the content and the way through it had to support the same understanding.

c.n: sub / Adapting the questions to the situation

c.tx: Adapting the questions to the situation

The screening questions at the beginning of the flow were intended to prevent unnecessary work later. A person whose circumstances made a set of questions irrelevant should not have to complete them simply because they appeared in a generic form.

I helped develop that direction into the prototype, alongside the prefilled information available through DÁP. These approaches addressed different sources of effort: screening limited the questions a person needed to answer, while prefilling reduced the information they needed to enter again. Both still required a clear and understandable journey.

The design judgement was in making the process appropriate to the user’s situation while retaining the information needed for administration. This connected interaction design with the underlying rules of the service.

c.n: sub / Making help and interruption part of the journey

c.tx: Making help and interruption part of the journey

I advocated for access to help throughout the process. The research had shown the uncertainty and stress that could accompany the task, so support needed to remain available while the user was working through it.

I also treated interruption as an expected part of the experience. Filling in a long application is tiring, and a person might give up partway through. Stopping did not have to mean losing the work: they could abort, and the answers completed so far went straight to the employment office, with an appointment booked to continue the registration in person.

The alternative was to complete every step online, after which only a short visit to sign remained. Either way, the person would see the office; what changed was how much was left to do there. The design therefore had to be considered alongside the legal discussion about when information could be prepared and when the employment office could receive it.

The intended benefit was continuity: effort already invested by the citizen remained useful even if they stopped early, and the appointment could start with much of the data already in place. The interface had to make the consequence of each route clear, rather than promise more than the service allowed.

Aligning the experience with service conditions

We held repeated discussions with ministry staff to align the proposed journey with their understanding of the process. A central topic was the legal timing of information handling: when could someone begin filling in their details, and when could those details reach the employment office?

This was directly relevant to the user experience. Preparing information, saving progress and sending information to an office cannot be treated as interchangeable actions. Their availability and explanation depend on what the administrative process permits.

My participation in this work connected the product design to that constraint. The aim was to retain a useful and understandable journey while adapting it to the institutional and legal conditions discussed by the wider team. Legal interpretation and final approval involved the relevant specialists and programme decision-makers.

The experience taught me to treat these conditions as design inputs from the beginning. The timing of an action can determine the structure of the journey, the meaning of a button and the expectation a person forms about what will happen next.

c.n: sub / Contributing to the service blueprint

c.tx: We also worked on a service blueprint to clarify different cases within the service. I contributed collaboratively, alongside the other disciplines involved in understanding the journey and its delivery.

The blueprint work sat alongside the research, ministry discussions and prototype development. Its contribution was to help clarify the service cases being considered as the concept became more detailed. It was part of the work required to relate the proposed citizen experience to the process around it.

My strongest hands-on responsibility remained the product experience. I used the broader service discussions as context for developing and iterating the prototype, rather than treating the screens as a self-contained solution.

c.n: sub / Iterating within shared decision making

c.tx: We developed the concept through research and institutional input, then iterated the prototype as the service understanding became more detailed. In that setting, my responsibility was to make the product implications concrete enough to examine and discuss.

I could take ownership of detailed design work while contributing to decisions shared across the team. The navigation and question structure were areas in which my contribution was particularly substantial. The wider service and programme decisions required agreement beyond the product-design pair.

Testing the prototype and assessing the outcome

c.n: sub / A detailed journey through a complex case

c.tx: A detailed journey through a complex case

The prototype followed a common but complex case. It gave us a connected journey through which to examine the navigation and the organisation of the questions. My work covered the navigation throughout that prototype, within the collaborative development and iteration of the wider design.

Using a complex case gave the concept enough substance to be tested as a journey. The prototype represented a selected scenario; it did not demonstrate every possible life situation or exception in the service.

We carried out usability testing on the prototype. My recollection is that most sessions went well and that participants generally welcomed the prospect of handling the process digitally. Some participants also gave detailed feedback on individual interface elements.

The positive response supported further development of the concept. It needed to be interpreted carefully: enthusiasm for digitalisation and usability of a particular flow are related but different observations. The sessions provided qualitative feedback on the prototype, rather than a measured improvement in the live service.

By the end of my involvement, the work had reached a detailed, iterated prototype supported by research and service-design work. My contribution connected interviewing and shared synthesis with hands-on product design, particularly navigation, question organisation and the experience of seeking help or interrupting the flow.

The team also produced extensive research documentation. That documentation was written by other colleagues; my role was in the research and design activities described here. The most direct evidence of my product work is the latest prototype from the period of my involvement.

Subsequent programme changes left the service’s rollout and eventual scope uncertain. I therefore describe the result at the level reached: a researched and tested service concept with a detailed prototype. There is no established live-service outcome here for processing time, completion rate or staff workload.

The project deepened my understanding of how legal and institutional conditions shape a public service. Knowing when a user can prepare information and when an authority can receive it affects the experience as directly as navigation or content structure. It also broadened my view of the people who might need the service. A single life event can contain very different circumstances and support needs. My contribution was to carry that understanding into concrete product decisions while working with the people responsible for research, service design, legal interpretation and approval.
